beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Rohan's phone buzzes. A message from his bank. Your home loan rate has been revised.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Handled the easy way, the interest on his loan goes from ₹83.7 L to ₹95.3 L.

beats.speaker: rohan
beats.say: Revised? Revised how? Nobody even asked me!

beats.speaker: priya
beats.say: They don't need your permission to change the rate. But how you pay for it is meant to be your choice, and the easy way is usually picked for you by default. Let's find out why.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: In October, the Reserve Bank of India raised the repo rate. That is the rate at which banks borrow from the RBI.

beats.speaker: sharma
beats.say: Think of the repo rate as a tap upstream. When the RBI turns it, every bank downstream feels the flow change.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Money costs banks more, so loans cost you more. Savers may earn a little more. Borrowers pay more.

beats.speaker: rohan
beats.say: But I signed my loan months ago. Why does a new decision touch my old loan?

beats.speaker: sharma
beats.say: Because your rate floats, beta. It was never fixed.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Most floating rate home loans from banks today are linked to an outside benchmark, very often the repo rate itself.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: On top of that, the bank adds its own margin, called the spread. The spread stays put. The benchmark moves.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: And the change does not land the same day. It lands on your reset date, which, for these loans, comes around at least once a quarter.

beats.speaker: priya
beats.say: So the hike reaches Rohan at his next reset. And then the question is, how does he pay for it?

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Rohan's loan is ₹60,00,000, over 300 months, at 8.4%. His EMI was ₹47,910.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Way one. Keep the same end date, and raise the EMI. At 8.65%, it becomes ₹48,922.

beats.speaker: rohan
beats.say: That's it? I'll hardly notice that.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Over the whole loan, though, his interest goes from ₹83.7 L to ₹86.8 L. Small each month, real money in total.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Way two. Leave the EMI almost exactly where it was, and add months at the end instead.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: At the new rate, the loan stretches from 300 months to 324. And the EMI? ₹47,926. It barely moves.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Extra months of EMIs, quietly added at the far end, years from now, right when Rohan expected to be free.

beats.speaker: rohan
beats.say: Same EMI? Perfect. And the bank already picked it for me!

beats.speaker: priya
beats.say: Rohan. The option that looks free is the expensive one.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Here is why. Every extra month is another month of interest on what he still owes. And in a loan's early years, most of each EMI is interest anyway.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Raise the EMI, and the total interest is ₹86.8 L. Stretch the loan, and it is ₹95.3 L.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: The choice that changed nothing on his monthly statement costs the most of all. It simply sends the bill to his future self.

beats.speaker: sharma
beats.say: In my bank days, a longer tenure was the easiest yes. Customers never complained. Most of them never even noticed.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: And it repeats. If rates rise again, the next hike can add more months on top of these.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Banks cannot stretch a loan forever. There is usually an age limit or a longest allowed term, and once that is reached, the EMI has to rise anyway.

beats.speaker: rohan
beats.say: Hold on. Was my bank supposed to ask me?

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Under RBI rules on interest rate resets, the bank has to tell you clearly, and let you choose. A higher EMI.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: A longer tenure. Or a mix of the two.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: The same rules let you ask to switch to a fixed rate, if your bank offers one, and to prepay part of the loan at any time.

beats.speaker: priya
beats.say: So the stretch is never your only option. You can just ask.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Now the twist. What if Rohan raises his EMI a little more than the bank asks for?

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Say he pays ₹50,891 a month, instead of ₹47,910. Same new rate, 8.65%.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Now his loan ends after 264 months. Years earlier than his original plan.

lines.text: less than ₹83.7 L before the hike

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: And his total interest falls to ₹74.4 L. That is less than the ₹83.7 L he was set to pay before the hike.

beats.speaker: rohan
beats.say: Wait. The hike made my loan cheaper?

beats.speaker: priya
beats.say: No. Paying faster made it cheaper. The hike just gave you a reason to start.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: One hike, three ways to handle it. Stretch the loan, ₹95.3 L. Raise the EMI to match, ₹86.8 L. Pay a little extra, ₹74.4 L.

beats.speaker: sharma
beats.say: But only if the budget truly allows it. An EMI you cannot keep up with is worse than any stretch.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: That is why an emergency fund comes first. Missing an EMI in a bad month costs far more than a little extra interest.

beats.speaker: priya
beats.say: So here is what Rohan does this week. Three steps.

items.text: Find your reset date and spread

beats.speaker: priya
beats.say: First. Find the reset date and the spread. They are in the loan letter, or in the bank's app.

items.text: Find your reset date and spread

beats.speaker: priya
beats.say: Second. After the reset, check what actually changed. The EMI, or the number of months left.

items.text: Find your reset date and spread

beats.speaker: priya
beats.say: Third. If the budget allows, he asks for a higher EMI instead of a longer loan.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: And if a bonus ever lands, prepaying part of a floating rate home loan generally carries no penalty for individual borrowers.

beats.speaker: rohan
beats.say: Calling the bank right now. EMI up. Not the months.

lines.text: The hike is paid either way

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: So. The repo rate went up, and your loan's cost went up with it. The only question is where you see it. Now, in your EMI. Or later, in years of extra payments.

params.cta: Check your loan's reset date this week
params.assumption: A ₹60,00,000 loan at 8.4%, rising to 8.65% from month one. Tenure rounded to whole months.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: These figures assume the full hike passes to the loan from its first month. Your bank's numbers will differ a little. Follow the panchayat for one money question, settled with real maths.
